note:
The chosen city of Zion, once exalted, has been humbled for her sins.

**1:1 How lonely.** The word “how” often begins biblical laments, contrasting the present disaster with previous prosperity. The first verse sets the theme of the lament: Jerusalem’s loss of greatness. The city, once favored, is desolate from the Babylonians’ plundering (Is. 1:21–26).

**widow.** Widowhood and solitude (Jer. 15:17) are typical pictures of abandonment. Israel’s husband is the Lord; she is therefore not a widow because of her husband’s death but because of the consequences of her unfaithfulness to God with her pagan lovers (see v. 2).

**slave.** Slavery is contrary to God’s ultimate design for Israel. They became a nation when God delivered them from slavery in Egypt so that they could serve Him (Deut. 6:20–25; Jer. 2:14; Deut. 15:12–18). The blessings of living in the Promised Land and serving according to the law are replaced with the punishments of exile and forced labor because the people have flagrantly and impenitently broken the covenant they accepted when they left Egypt (Ex. 24:7, 8; Deut. 28:47–50).

A word often used ironically in reference to Judah’s idolatrous neighbors, with whom she has consorted willingly (Jer. 3:1).

**none to comfort.** See also vv. 7, 9, 16; cf. the comfort promised in Is. 40:1. Here there is no limit to the effects of the Babylonian ravages.

**friends.** Her former allies who have abandoned her in her hour of need.

For the fall of Judah, see 2 Kin. 24:20–25:30; Jer. 39–45, 52.

**exile.** The ultimate humiliation for the covenant people (Deut. 28:63–68).

**no resting place.** The Lord promised and provided His people rest from their enemies (Deut. 12:9; 2 Sam. 7:1, cf. Deut. 28:65). Israel and Judah’s unfaithfulness has left them without rest.

A picture of ancient Israel’s regular worship life.

**roads to Zion.** In the past, people who lived at a distance would travel these roads in pilgrimage to the temple (Ps. 84:5), but now that temple has been destroyed by the Babylonians.

**festival.** The three main yearly gatherings for worship are Unleavened Bread/Passover, Weeks (Pentecost), and Booths (Ex. 23:14–17; Lev. 23:4–44). Under normal circumstances, Jerusalem is crowded, and priests preside over the vibrant celebrations. The exile now makes this impossible.

**her priests groan.** The priests are those most affected by the destruction of the temple.

**virgins have been afflicted.** A sign of defeat; cf. Jer. 31:13.

See other complaints in Jer. 12:1; Ps. 73. Here the complaint comes with a confession of sin. As the Prophets foretold, Judah’s unfaithfulness has brought her to grief.

**the Lord has afflicted her.** Jerusalem’s destruction is not the result of the great power of the Babylonians and their gods; it is the Lord’s judgment upon the people. In this lay their hope: the One who has wounded them can bind up those wounds (see Hos. 6:1).Their Judge’s covenant faithfulness endures forever (see 3:22–24).

This phrase personifies Jerusalem (Jer. 6:2), but it might also allude to the women of the city, who feel its anguish most keenly.

**all her majesty has departed.** The glory of God, which once inhabited the Most Holy Place of the temple in Jerusalem, has abandoned it and gone into exile with those in Babylon (see Ezek. 8–11).

The bitter present contrasts with an earlier, happier time, possibly the days of David and Solomon.

**none to help her.** Cf. Ps. 46:5.

The idea that sin has caused the exile is developed, first with images of ritual impurity.

**filthy.** Probably refers to menstruation, which, like other bodily emissions of life fluids, renders a person temporarily unfit to stand in God’s presence (Lev. 15:19–33). The consequence of Judah’s sin is similar, if not more severe: being cut off from God’s worship, and perhaps also suffering public humiliation (cf. Jer. 13:22, 26). Jerusalem’s spiritual adultery, in which she has stripped before her lovers, is fittingly punished by an unwilling uncovering. In the day Lamentations is written, prisoners of war, both male and female, are often stripped naked as an act of extreme humiliation. Cf. a similar sequence in Ezek. 16:36–39.

The image of ritual uncleanness intensifies.

**she has no comforter.** Since she has been deaf to the warnings of His prophets, the Lord is deaf to her appeals (see Jer. 11:11).

**O Lord, behold.** An element of appeal to the Lord, a normal part of the lament form (Introduction: Characteristics and Primary Themes), is now introduced.

The temple’s true purpose is to attract the nations to worship the God of Israel (1 Kin. 8:41–43), but now it has brought invaders who desecrate it.

**those whom you forbade.** Since God’s people have not protected the sanctity of the temple but allowed uncircumcised Gentiles to enter it (see Ezek. 44:6–8), God has brought Gentiles to destroy it.
This vivid picture of desolation hints at food shortages.

verse_quote: all you who pass by ... like my sorrow.
note:
The sufferer imagines that his suffering is unprecedented. Yet no one seems to sympathize.

**the day of his fierce anger.** A grim confirmation of Amos’s prophecy that on the day of the Lord His anger will be against His own people (Amos 5:18).

verse_quote: From on high he sent fire.
note:
Zion knows that the Lord Himself has afflicted her (Ps. 88:13–18). Her downfall is like that of Sodom and Gomorrah (Gen. 19:24).

**he spread a net.** Cf. Ezek. 17:20.
See Jer. 27, 28.
The Lord, formerly a warrior on Israel’s behalf (Deut. 9:1–3), has turned His might against His own people, trampling her like grapes in a winepress (see Is. 63:1–4).

See Jer. 9:1.

**a comforter is far from me.** There is no one to help, no one to comfort—a dominant theme in these verses (2, 7, 9, 17).

A historic name for Israel, derived from the name of the nation’s ancestor (Gen. 32:28).

**his neighbors should be his foes.** The presence of Judah as an unclean thing among the nations falsifies her intended role as a witness to the holiness of God (Ex. 19:5, 6).

verse_quote: The Lord is in the right.
note: Zion justifies the Lord’s punishment by an admission of sin (see Ps. 51:4). Yet the thought shifts quickly again to her slavery.

The nations around Judah fail to help her in her time of need.

**priests and elders.** See Jer. 2:8.

Zion appeals to the Lord because of her enemies’ gloating. Their insults are deeply offensive to Judah’s status as God’s covenant people—and therefore to God Himself. According to the Abrahamic covenant, their insults demand a divine response (Gen. 12:1–3).

**day.** The day of the Lord now becomes a day of terror for Zion’s enemies. Zion’s lament follows an established prophetic pattern: the enemies who administer God’s judgment finally come to suffer judgment themselves (Jer. 25:15–38).

Zion finally asserts that her enemies merit judgment as much as she does.

**my groans.** The petition to punish, however, does not diminish Zion’s deep distress.

The second lament over Zion’s loss of glory begins, and the poet portrays the Lord’s anger with her.

**2:1 How.** Cf. 1:1 and note.

**He has cast down ... the splendor.** Israel’s fall into disfavor is compared to a falling star (Is. 14:12).

**has not remembered.** Judah is astonished that the promise to David is now apparently void (cf. Ps. 89, especially vv. 38–51). Isaiah assured the people that God would protect Zion (e.g., Is. 37:35), and the people of Judah has absolutized these promises, forgetting their obligation to keep the terms of God’s covenant with them (Ex. 24:1–3).

**his footstool.** A term normally used for the ark of the covenant (1 Chr. 28:2; Ps. 132:7) or for the earth (Is. 66:1). It is here applied to Zion (cf. Ps. 99:5).

Cf. Ex. 34:6, 7.

**strongholds.** The strength of the fortified cities of Judah once symbolized God’s blessing in response to Judah’s covenant faithfulness (2 Chr. 10:4–12).

The language vividly contrasts Judah and her enemies, as well as Judah’s life as it should be and as it is.

**a flaming fire ... consuming all around.** Cf. Ex. 3:2.

The harmful arrows meant for God’s enemies (Deut. 32:42) are now aimed at His people (Hos. 5:10; Jer. 6:11; 7:20).

**like an enemy.** See note on 1:15.

**poured out his fury.** This holy war imagery is classically used of God’s judgment on the nations (Ps. 69:24).
See note on 1:6.

References to the temple.

**the Lord has made ... forget festival and Sabbath.** See note on 1:4. This can be rendered “The Lord has made appointed feasts and Sabbaths forgotten things in Zion,” an ironic justice since the people first forgot the Sabbaths themselves (Amos 8:5; Jer. 17:19–27).

**king and priest.** The Lord’s wrath is poured out on the sacred place, the sacred festivals, and the sacred people. Everything holy is swept away by His wrath.
God’s judgment destroys not only the place of His dwelling, but Israel’s means of approaching Him in worship. The shouts of triumphant enemies replace the cry of worshiping assemblies.
To survey the city for destruction (Is. 34:11; Amos 7:7, 8). In Zech. 1:16, the Lord promises to do the same thing when He restores His chosen city.
Not only are the religious institutions destroyed, but the Lord withholds revelation. The prophetic vision that accompanies preaching of the law has ceased (Jer. 8:8–10; 18:18; 1 Sam. 3:1).

verse_quote: The elders ... dust ... sackcloth ... bowed their heads.
note:
Conventional gestures of mourning (1:14; Job 2:12, 13). Here they are undertaken by old men and young women, implying the comprehensiveness of the mourning.

**2:11 My eyes are spent with weeping.** Cf. this natural suffering because of the agony of his people with Jer. 4:19, and note the pictures of desolation that accompany the prophet’s expressions of anguish (Jer. 4:31).

**my bile.** Lit. “my liver,” which in Hebrew thought is one of the key locations of the emotions.
The poet is especially moved by the sight of suffering children., 12

verse_quote: What can I say for you.
note:
The meaning seems to be, “What can I tell you about suffering, you who have suffered so much?” No ready answers occur to someone who has witnessed sorrows such as these.

**comfort.** See note on 1:2.

The thought advances from v. 9; prophets are now said to have prophesied falsely. The complex problem of false prophecy is a recurrent theme of the Prophets (Jer. 5:12, 13; 23:9–40; 28). Deut. 18:21, 22 furnishes one of the criteria by which prophets may be judged true or false.

verse_quote: perfection of beauty ... joy of all the earth.
note: The beauty of the chosen place is extravagantly expressed (Pss. 50:2; 48:2), but it is by scoffers who mock the ruin and agony of Jerusalem.

In vv. 2 and 5, God Himself is said to have swallowed up the people. As this verse makes clear, He has done this using Judah’s enemies as His agents. The verse also shows how the nations proudly attribute their victory over Judah to their own strength.

verse_quote: carried out his word ... commanded long ago.
note:
God’s purposes of judgment were declared via Moses in the curses of the covenant (Lev. 26:23–39; Deut. 28:15–68). Judah’s present has happened in accordance with God’s known purposes. See 1:18; 2:8.

**might.** See note on v. 3.

There is irony in this futile cry to the city wall, a symbol of the nation’s imagined strength.

**day and night.** Cf. Deut. 28:67.
See note on v. 12.

The theme of the suffering of innocent children reaches the height of pathos (Jer. 19:9). Its power as an appeal to God is enhanced by the knowledge that God knows motherly affection (Is. 66:13). As extreme in its own way is the outrage of sacrilege: the Lord’s anointed ones are killed in His sanctuary. This is only possible because the temple in Jerusalem has already been desecrated by the people’s idolatry (see Ezek. 8; 9).

**priest and prophet.** For the sins of priests and prophets, see 4:13.
The horror of death in youth contrasts with the blessing of attaining a good age (Job 42:17).

This contrast between summoning to the joy of a feast and summoning to disaster is starkly powerful.

**terrors on every side.** See Jer. 6:25; 20:10.

**day of the anger of the Lord.** The poem ends where it began—without alleviation of the dark picture.

As an individual expresses the grief of the community, hope and consolation are sustained by a knowledge of God’s compassionate love. This central chapter is three times as long as each of the surrounding chapters, highlighting its importance.

**3:1 I am the man.** This chapter is an acrostic with three verses for each letter of the Hebrew alphabet. On the poet’s possible identity as Jeremiah, and the acrostic form in Hebrew poetry, see Introduction: Author; Introduction: Genre and Literary Features; and the notes below. For portrayals of the Lord Himself as the One who has afflicted the speaker, see Job 19:21; Ps. 88:7, 15; Jer. 15:17, 18. In this poem, an individual expresses the grief of his community (vv. 40–54).

Cf. Is. 9:2. Darkness is a metaphor for the distress experienced in the absence of God; light stands for the opposite: salvation and blessing. The day of the Lord is described in these terms at Amos 5:18.
Pictures of physical distress, perhaps due to age or illness (Job 13:28; Is. 38:13). For broken bones as a picture of judgment, see Ps. 51:8.
The emotional and physical effects of distress go hand in hand.

Distress and disease diminish life’s fullness, culminating in death. In his weakened condition, the poet considers himself to have little more participation in life than he would if he were actually dead. From the perspective of the living, the dead exist not at all, or only as shadows (Prov. 2:18; 9:18 and notes). For other pictures of death in the OT, see Job 3:11–19; Pss. 6:5; 115:17; Is. 14:18, 19; Ezek. 32:17–32. Against this background, the OT is eloquent in its brief testimony to resurrection beyond the grave (Job 19:25–27; Pss. 16:9–11; 49:15; 73:24; Dan. 12:2).
For unheard prayer see Pss. 10:1; 13:1; 22:1, 2; and especially Jer. 7:16.

verse_quote: he has made my paths crooked.
note: In Jer. 3:21, the people have made their own way crooked, so the punishment matches the crime.
Some of the hazards that can actually overtake the traveler are vivid ways of expressing terror and distress. For the Lord as an archer, see 2:4.
See Jer. 20:7.
See Jer. 9:15.
These conditions, the sum of blessing, are completely absent.
The expression of hopelessness in the poem reaches its climax here.
The Lord has not remembered Jerusalem, His footstool (see 2:1).
The poet’s experience is a symbol of the people’s; see 1:7.

Memory that once discouraged now encourages (Ps. 77:3–9, 10–15). The memory of God’s devotion to His people brings hope out of hopelessness. This hope is only possible if God is the One who sovereignly afflicts and sovereignly heals.

The climactic point of the poem and the book. The lament form often has turning points where the experience of rejection by God turns unexpectedly to confidence, based on a knowledge of His character and of His past mercies. See the confessions of trust and hope in Ps. 22.

**3:22, 23** See theological note “The Goodness of God” on p. 991.

**3:22 steadfast love.** On the Hb. word (_hesed_), see note on Ps. 36:5. The plural form, used here, recalls many acts or perhaps the riches of divine love. Cf. Is. 55:3.

**mercies.** God’s covenant devotion is always joined with His compassion. Though the Lord may withhold mercy temporarily (see 2:2), that is not the end of the story. His people are not finally consumed because God’s compassion is not consumed. God’s wrath toward His people must come to an end because His compassion cannot end (4:22; Hos. 11:8).

**3:23 every morning.** God’s love will bring the morning of salvation (Pss. 30:5; 90:14; Mal. 4:2; Luke 1:78).

**your faithfulness.** The poet switches to the second person here rather than continuing to speak about God in the third person. Addressing God so directly marks intimacy and directness. God’s unqualified reliability makes Him worthy of faith (Hab. 2:4).
This phrase recalls the territorial allocations to the Israelite tribes. The priests and Levites, who are landless, have the Lord as their portion (Num. 18:20; cf. Ps. 73:26).

God is always good to those who seek, hope, and wait for Him (cf. 1 Chr. 28:9). The threefold “good” in this context (cf. vv. 26, 27) focuses attention on God’s goodness. Since God is good, His people may wait quietly for His deliverance even when they do not understand His purposes.

If a man suffers in early and middle life, he at least faces the possibility of relief in old age. Perhaps the community, like an individual, should hope for the yoke to be lifted with the passage of time.

The poet exhorts the afflicted to bear present suffering in light of the affirmation in the next verses.

**3:28 sit alone.** Cf. 1:1.
The poet urges a humble submissiveness before the oppressor, since the judgment ultimately comes from the Lord. Israel’s humiliation foreshadows Christ’s humiliation (Is. 50:6; Matt. 26:67).

Since God is compassionate, the present experience of His wrath must be temporary (Ps. 30:5; Is. 54:7; Hos. 6:1). Again, compassion is joined to God’s unfailing love (Hb. _hesed,_ 3:22). Even in judgment, God does not afflict people “willingly,” that is, “cheerfully” or “from His heart.” He takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked (Ezek. 18:23).

The implication of these verses is that God cannot ultimately approve of such things (Job 8:3). The Babylonians will pay for their arrogant assault on the Lord’s people (cf. Jer. 50; 51). Of course, in another sense, God has approved these very things, since He has brought them to pass. This is the problem of judgment and affliction that the poet faces: God can ordain and use things that He hates in order to accomplish things that He loves.
All that happens is by God’s word (Gen. 1:3), calamity as well as good (Amos 3:6)., 38

Since all things take place by the word of the Lord, no one can complain when God brings calamity as punishment for sin. The sin of the people is an important part of the poet’s answer to the problem of judgment and affliction (dreadful though God’s judgment is; cf. 2:20–22). The phrase in Hebrew implies that sin and consequent punishment belong inseparably together.

The speaker uses plural subject forms throughout this section. The poet speaks as the representative of his people.

**3:40–42 Let us test ... transgressed.** A call to repentance, acknowledging sin. The impulse to confess sins seems to give way soon to renewed lamentation, following the statement “you have not forgiven” (v. 42). The penalties for sin are not yet lifted.

verse_quote: lift up our hearts and hands.
note: Internal and external signs of repentance.

verse_quote: You have wrapped ... among the peoples.
note: The poet parodies the actions of God at the exodus. Then, God’s anger helped Israel; it was her enemies who were slain without pity. Then, the cloud was a sign of favor. Israel was precious among the nations, not “scum and garbage.”

The poet returns to singular subject forms.

**3:48 rivers of tears.** There are strong echoes of Jeremiah in this close association between the people’s grief and the poet’s grief (see Jer. 9:1). A link is suggested between the suffering of the people and of the poet.
Familiar language of lament (Pss. 6:6; 42:3; Jer. 9:1; 18).

verse_quote: until the Lord from heaven looks down and sees.
note: See Is. 63:15.
See Ps. 35:19; John 15:25.
Pss. 28:1; 88:6. Jeremiah’s life may here be in view (Jer. 38:6), though the metaphor is also common in the book of Psalms.

See Pss. 16:10, 11; 30:1; and Jonah’s experience (Jon. 2:2–7). Christ’s suffering, death, and resurrection as the righteous Servant of the Lord brings this recurring theme of the suffering prophet and his rescue by God to its highest fulfillment.
The turning point of the lament arrives when the poet is reassured that the Lord has heard his prayer (Ps. 6:8–10).
A common exhortation in Isaiah (e.g., Is. 41:10; cf. Mark 6:50).

This section takes up the biblical theme of innocent, vicarious suffering that reaches its consummation in Christ’s death for those who bring it upon Him.

**3:58–60 my cause ... redeemed my life ... my cause.** In Jer. 50:34, the Lord is Judah’s redeemer, and He pleads the people’s case. Here the Lord pleads against them, because they have turned against His prophet.
The intervention for which the poet prays in Jer. 12:1, as in Ps. 77:6, 7. If the Lord is just, He must act in defense of His servant.

This chapter, containing the most vivid portrayal of Judah’s agonies, laments Zion’s punishment but gives assurances that the punishment will cease.

**4:1 the gold ... The holy stones.** The gold and the rich furnishings of Solomon’s temple have been laid waste by Nebuchadnezzar (2 Kin. 25:9).

The idea of gold is quickly transferred to the people themselves, who are more valuable than the temple’s riches. As God’s “treasured possession” (Ex. 19:5), they were once exceedingly precious; now they are the most common clay, ready to be smashed (see Jer. 19).

Jackals are regarded as scavengers, but at least they care for their own young. Under the enormous stress of the siege, the people of Jerusalem didn’t care for their children.

**ostriches.** Proverbial figures for the callousness of parents toward their children (Job 39:13–17). This indifference is a theme of the chapter (v. 10), developed from 2:20.

The picture of someone rich and delicately bred falling suddenly into dire want and danger is echoed often in the Prophets (Amos 4:1–3; 6:1; Jer. 6:2).

**purple.** Because of the limited supply of the dye, only the very rich in the poet’s day can afford purple.

According to the context, the Hb. word can be translated “punishment” or “iniquity” because the two ideas are intimately linked. The connection is strong in this chapter, where Judah’s intense suffering is linked repeatedly to her unnatural sin.

**Sodom.** The Prophets often use Sodom as an archetype of divine judgment on sin (Deut. 29:23; Is. 1:9, 10; Jer. 23:14; Ezek. 16:46; Hos. 11:8; Amos 4:11; Luke 17:28–30). The comparison with Sodom holds for the sins of the city as well for the dreadful judgment that fell upon it.

Hb. _nazir_ means “consecrated one”; see note on Num. 6:1–21.

**whiter ... ruddy.** Colors often associated with the human body. Light-colored skin is a sign of wealth, since laborers work out in the sun and are tanned by the sun.
In the prevailing difficulties, no one is marked out as special; all distinctions have been obliterated. Those who once were proud of their appearance are unrecognizable.
The people’s misery is desperate and wretched. Death by famine is not an instant judgment; in its lingering, it exposes the horrors of God’s judgment to a dreadful degree (Deut. 28:54–57).
See v. 3. One of the sins for which Jeremiah repeatedly rebuked the people before the fall of Jerusalem was child sacrifice (e.g., Jer. 7:31); thus, in an awful way, the punishment fits the crime.
The focus returns to God’s wrath. Judah’s sin—and the Lord’s righteous punishment—provides the explanation for the ills that the people are suffering.

Possibly refers to the assumed impregnability of Zion, reinforced by the dramatic failure of the Assyrians to take the city after Sennacherib’s conquest of the rest of Judah in 701 B.C. (2 Kin. 18:13–19:37).
See notes on 2:20 and Jer. 5:30, 31; Mic. 3:9–12.

Deut. 28:28, 29.

**defiled with blood.** God, in His wrath, has made Zion’s priests and prophets ritually unclean. As elsewhere (Is. 59:3), the phrase refers to blood spilled by the guilty. By their complicity in the sins of others, the priests and prophets have become defiled.

See Lev. 13:45. Earlier the people welcomed the false prophets and their message of peace, but now they shun them like lepers.

**fugitives.** The curse of Deut. 28:65, 66 is fulfilled.

Israel and Judah characteristically sought help in political alliances rather than in the Lord (Is. 7; 30:1–5; Jer. 24). Just prior to Nebuchadnez­zar’s siege of Jerusalem, their hopes were pinned on receiving assistance from Egypt (Jer. 37:5–10), but the fall of the city has proven those hopes ill-founded.
See Ezek. 7:6.
See Jer. 4:13. When the remnant tried to escape Jerusalem after its walls were breached, there was nowhere safe to run.

verse_quote: The breath of our nostrils, the Lord’s anointed.
note: The Davidic king is the psychological center for the people, the embodiment of the Lord’s ancient promise to David (2 Sam. 7). The last king of Judah, deported by Nebuchadnezzar, was Zedekiah (2 Kin. 25:7). Although the Lord declared an end to the immediate rule of that line in the days of Jehoiachin, Zedekiah’s predecessor (Jer. 22:28–30), He at the same time promised final salvation through the righteous Branch of David, the Messiah (Jer. 23:5–8).

One of Israel’s historic enemies, who aided the Babylonians in their assault on Jerusalem and turned over fugitives (see Obad. 14). Her enmity is the more scandalous because of an ancient affinity of blood; Edom is another name for Jacob’s brother, Esau (Gen. 25:30). But the nation of Edom will also fall in its turn (see Obadiah and Jer. 49:7–22).

**4:22 The punishment of your iniquity ... is accomplished.** That is, “Your guilt will end.” Because of God’s mercy and compassion, the guilt of His people will be ended, and they, in contrast to Edom, will be delivered to rebuild their ruined land. See Is. 40:2 and Jer. 49:7–22.

Rehearsing the continuing effects of Zion’s degradation, the poet makes a final plea for restoration.

**5:1 Remember ... us.** A typical opening for a communal lament. Zion no longer appears in the immediate throes of siege and plunder (as in ch. 4) but at a later stage of affliction, when the sudden violation of the land has given way to harsh and humiliating oppression. “Remembering” in the Bible is never simply recalling a thought; it implies the appropriate action as well (cf. Deut. 6:4–9; Ps. 78).

The land as a whole is Israel’s inheritance from God (Deut. 4:21; 12:9), while the territory of Judah is given specifically to the tribe of that name (Josh. 15:20–63).

**strangers ... foreigners.** God gave the land to Israel, and even directed her to expel the foreigners. Now the situation is reversed.

Their position is precarious and dependent. Israel is commanded in the Mosaic law to show care for them because their condition denies them normal access to the land’s goods (Deut. 14:28, 29). Yet, paradoxically, that the nation has become one of orphans and widows is good news, for the Lord shows special care for these needy groups (see Ps. 146:9).

verse_quote: We must pay for the water.
note: This necessity is an ironic reversal of Deut. 6:10, 11 and especially Josh. 9:21–23.
This condition is another reversal of a blessing promised in Deuteronomy (Deut. 12:9; Lam. 1:3).
This kind of submission is not only humiliating but dangerous (2 Kin. 18:14). It continues to be a temptation even after Jerusalem’s fall. See Jer. 41–44.

verse_quote: Our fathers sinned ... we bear their iniquities.
note: A similar description of solidarity between generations is found in Ex. 20:5 and in the books of 1 and 2 Kings, with their records of guilt accumulated over the generations. Passages such as Ezek. 18 (notes; Jer. 31:29, 30) address those who question the justice of being judged for sins they have not committed. Ezekiel answers that those who share in their father’s judgment have shared in their father’s sins; each generation bears the guilt of its own sins, not just the guilt of the sins of previous generations.

When Babylonian servants command Israel, the true relationships between God, Israel, and the nations has ironically been distorted. Israel is in truth a nation freed from slavery (Deut. 15:12–18); but those who do not serve the true God must be in bondage. See 1:1 and note.
Possibly speaks of wilderness robbers who have taken advantage of the weakened community. Much of the land is depopulated during the Babylonian exile.
One of the consequences of malnutrition.

Pictures of shame and lawlessness in the absence of authority figures.

**5:11 young women.** The loss of virginity outside marriage brings shame on a woman and her family, and possibly additional serious consequences (Deut. 22:13–21).
A form of torture or of execution by exposure.
Degrading toil for a young man (Judg. 16:21).

This verse conveys something of the state of normal life in Judah by describing what has ceased. The “gate,” which has legal and social functions, is now deserted. The lighthearted pleasures of the “young men” have been replaced by the harsh life depicted in the preceding verses.

verse_quote: our dancing has been turned to mourning.
note: In this culture, dancing is the outward manifestation of joy in the same way that mourning is the outward manifestation of grief.

Some take this to refer to Jerusalem in particular (1:1; 2:15; 5:18). Probably it represents the glory of Israel and Judah among the nations (Ex. 19:6).

**woe ... sinned.** See note on v. 7.

The poet comes full circle from 1:1, resuming the theme of the scandal of the chosen city of God lying destroyed and abandoned. In the poet’s era, jackals typically scavenge around empty ruins (see Jer. 9:11).

Though the “royalty” of the people (v. 16) is no more, that of the Lord remains forever. This is particularly poignant since the reign of the earthly son of David and of the Lord are often associated in the book of Psalms (e.g., Ps. 45:5, 6).

The note of lament is struck again. There is no easy exit from the pain that has been expressed, but the affirmation of God’s sovereignty is made in the midst of that pain (v. 19). The logic of vv. 19, 20 is paralleled in Ps. 89, where vv. 1–37 praise God’s sovereignty and vv. 38–51 ask “How long?” Has the Lord, who reigns forever, forgotten His people forever?

These two words are from the same Hb. verb. Its use is ambiguous, since the restoration can be either a physical return of exiles to the land or a return that is moral and religious (repentance). The ambiguity is necessary because the Prophets never envisage a restoration to the land that is separate from repentance toward God. For an exact parallel of this thought, see Jer. 31:18.

The poet declines to finish the lament on a high note, for it is the Lord, not he, who is sovereign. Nevertheless, the final note is not one of despair but of petition. The five poems in the book come to us out of the acute grief of the judgment experienced, but they also point to the compassion of God as grounds for the hope of future deliverance.
